l3hu-bn-aggression: HU Button: The Frequency Advantage of Acting Last Preflop

In heads-up, the button (SB) acts last preflop every hand — a frequency advantage you enjoy every single hand. With only one opponent, you can open with about 80% of hands — any pair, any Ax, and suited connectors all play. The key isn't "stronger cards" but "higher frequency": you seize the initiative, keep the opponent responding passively, and his defense cost rises quickly with your aggression.

Button aggression isn't "playing looser" but "seizing the initiative more actively". Every hand you act last preflop, meaning you have one more piece of information than the BB — use it to pressure constantly, not waste it waiting for good cards.
Postflop Pressure: C-Bet Frequency and Size

Postflop you (SB) act first (position reversal, OOP), but preflop initiative still makes the C-Bet valuable. HU C-Bet frequency is far higher than full ring: because the opponent's defense range is wide and hit rates low, your consecutive bets steal pots at high frequency. On dry high boards use 1/3-pot small bets at high frequency (about 70%-80%); on wet connected boards use 2/3+ pot big bets to protect equity. The key — HU C-Bet value is "making the wide-range weak hands fold + thin value", not "representing strength".

Example: HU 100BB deep, you (SB) hold A♠5♠ and min-raise to 2BB, BB calls, pot 4BB. Flop K♠7♦2♣. You're the preflop aggressor but OOP postflop. On this dry high board the BB's range rarely hits a K, so you bet 1/3 pot about 1.3BB: A5's overcards + backdoor flush have enough equity to support continued pressure while making the BB's junk pay. If he folds you win 4BB directly; if he calls you have the A-high as later improvement.

Counterintuitive point: "constant pressure" on the HU button doesn't mean "bet every street". Postflop you're OOP (act first); on wet boards or when the turn changes hands, mix in checks to keep the check-raise (x/r) lever. Aggression is a frequency advantage, not mindless firing.

Button aggression quick memory: open about 80% preflop, C-Bet about 70%-80% (1/3 pot) on dry postflop boards, lower frequency with big sizes on wet boards. Every 50 hands check: is your C-Bet frequency too low, letting the BB check-float endlessly? Is your open too tight, wasting the act-last advantage?
l3hu-sb-continuation: The SB's C-Bet: OOP Continuation-Bet Discipline

In heads-up the SB acts first postflop (OOP), meaning your C-Bet isn't "representing strength" but "using the right range and size to make the wide-range BB fold or pay". Unlike the full-ring BTN, the SB's C-Bet costs more against the IP BB: you're torn when raised. So the SB's C-Bet range relies more on board and range advantage — high frequency on dry high boards, lower on wet connected boards, mixing checks to keep the x/r lever.

The core OOP C-Bet discipline: first judge "whose range does this board hit". Dry boards → SB range advantage → high-frequency small bets; wet boards → BB nut advantage → lower frequency and pot control. Don't fire mindlessly because "I'm the aggressor".
Size and Range: When to Continue, When to Check

The SB's postflop continuation choices have three tiers: (1) dry high boards (like K♠7♦2♣) — the SB's opening range holds plenty of Kx with clear range advantage, so C-Bet at high frequency (about 70%-80%) with 1/3-pot small bets, making the BB's wide-range weak hands fold or betting thin value; (2) wet connected boards (like 9♠8♥6♣) — the BB's defense range holds many straights/draws with the nut advantage tilted to the BB, so the SB lowers frequency (about 30%-40%) and mixes checks; (3) neutral boards without range advantage — the SB check-calls with small/medium pairs and check-raises with strong draws, building a balanced range.

Example: HU 100BB deep, you (SB) min-raise to 2BB, BB calls, pot 4BB. Flop Q♦8♣3♠ (dry). You're OOP. Your opening range holds plenty of Qx and the BB's defense range rarely hits a Q — range advantage yours. Bet 1/3 pot about 1.3BB: QJ/QT thin value, A-high semi-bluffs, small pairs also bet — the whole range C-Bets at high frequency and the BB's weak hands can only fold.

Example 2 (wet-board frequency drop): Same pot, flop 9♠8♥6♣. The BB's defense range holds 87/65/97 and many straights/draws — nut advantage tilts to the BB. You hold K♠K♦ (overpair): still ahead but easily outdrawn, so bet 2/3 pot to protect equity, but A-high and small pairs should check for pot control — the SB's C-Bet frequency drops sharply on this board.

Counterintuitive point: an OOP C-Bet isn't "declaring initiative". When the preflop aggressor is OOP postflop, a check isn't weakness but handing the decision to the IP and deciding whether to accept. Mixing checks to keep the x/r lever is the mature HU SB play.

SB C-Bet decision three questions: (1) whose range does this board hit? (2) is my hand value, semi-bluff, or pure air? (3) can I handle being raised? After three questions, OOP continuation betting goes from habit to structure.
l3hu-bb-defense: BB: The Best-Positioned But Heaviest-Defending Seat in HU

The HU BB is the postflop positional-advantage side (IP), but faces the SB's attack every hand preflop, defending at 60%+. This "60%+ defense" isn't passive calling but structured defense: a call pile (small/medium pairs, suited connectors, weak Ax) + a 3Bet value pile (strong hands for value) + a 3Bet bluff pile (blockers). Because the BB is IP postflop and the SB's 0.5 dead money makes calls cheap, marginal hands can defend profitably.

The BB's "60%+ defense" is defense with position: acting last preflop + acting last postflop make calling marginal hands far cheaper than full ring. Transplanting the full-ring "BB must play tight" into HU throws away positional advantage.

Postflop IP, the BB faces the SB's C-Bet with three choices: call, raise, or fold. The check-raise (x/r) is the key tool for building the BB's range — using strong hands + strong draws to form a polarized x/r range, suppressing the SB's C-Bet frequency and protecting the calling range from exploitation. The x/r math: when the SB's C-Bet frequency is too high and his fold rate insufficient, the BB's x/r semi-bluff auto-profits.

Example: HU 100BB deep, SB min-raises to 2BB, you (BB) call with 7♠6♠, pot 4BB. Flop 8♣5♦2♠. SB C-Bets 1.3BB (half pot). You have a double-gutshot (4 sixes + 4 nines) + backdoor flush — a standard x/r semi-bluff. Raise to about 4BB: if the SB folds you win 5.3BB directly; if called you have 8+ outs of improvement. The x/r both protects your draw and makes the SB's wide-range C-Bet pay.

Example 2 (disadvantaged-position control): Same pot, you (BB) hold A♠K♠ on a K♦8♣3♥ flop (dry top pair). You're IP; the SB C-Bets 1.3BB. Top pair top kicker on a dry board tends toward calling rather than raising — calling keeps the SB's bluffs while you control later streets in position. An x/r instead scares off the SB's weak hands, wasting top pair's thin value. The IP advantage is "calling to watch the opponent keep firing, or betting thin value yourself".

Counterintuitive point: wide BB defense isn't a calling station. A real station has no x/r and no 3Bet pile; the HU BB's 60% consists of calls, 3Bet value, 3Bet bluffs, and x/r — each moving with the SB's tendencies. Defense width and defense passivity are two different things.

BB defense three-step quick check: (1) call the pot odds — calling line about 33% vs a 2BB SB open; (2) split piles — strong made hands 3Bet value, blockers 3Bet bluff, medium hands call; (3) watch the SB — raise 3Bet vs an over-folder, raise isolate vs a big limper, raise x/r vs an over-frequent C-Better.
l4hu-bn-opening: Opening Near 100%: The HU Button's Offense

The HU button (SB) acts last preflop; against the single opponent, the opening frequency can approach 100% — only a few completely junk hands (like 72o, 83o) fold. Because: the SB completes 0.5 to see a 1.5BB pot (25% required equity), and any hand against the BB's wide defense range is near or above that line; plus acting last preflop means you always have the initiative. High-frequency opening isn't "playing loose" but "using frequency to squeeze every marginal EV".

The core of button opening is "sizing serves postflop", not "sizing serves the steal". In HU use min-raise (2BB) as the main weapon: the steal bar is low (needs 60% fold rate), the small size makes postflop pot control easier, and a wide enough range covers various boards.
Opening-Size Math: Why Min-Raise Is the Main Weapon

SB min-raise to 2BB math (SB already posted 0.5, extra risk 1.5BB; BB posted 1, can fold or complete 1):

Pure steal model: SB extra risk 1.5BB, target prize 1BB
EV(raise) = f×1 − (1−f)×1.5 (f = BB fold rate)
Break-even: f = 1.5/2.5 = 60%

So if the BB folds more than 60%, the SB's min-raise with any two cards auto-profits.
Size comparison: min-raise 2BB → 60%; 2.5BB → 66.7%; 3BB → 71.4%.

Conclusion: the smaller the size, the lower the auto-profit bar. In HU the open's value is postflop, and the smaller the size the easier pot control.

Why doesn't HU use full ring's "bigger sizes to steal"? Three points: (1) the real HU BB fold rate vs min-raise is only about 30%-40%, so pure stealing barely profits — the value is postflop; (2) big sizes are "self-punishment" in HU — the BB's calling range narrows with size, so spending 3BB only buys a stronger, in-position calling range; (3) frequency and balance — min-raise lets you open about 80% of hands, and only a wide enough range covers various postflop boards.

Example: HU 100BB deep, you (SB) hold Q♦J♦. This is a marginal full-ring tight-position hand, but in HU QJs has about 52% equity vs the BB's wide defense range — min-raise 2BB is the standard open. Postflop you have flush/straight-draw potential plus the SB's act-last advantage; QJs is an absolute open on the HU button.

Example 2 (sizing adjusts to the opponent): You observe the BB folds to min-raises at 55%. Even then the min-raise's pure-steal EV = 0.55×1 − 0.45×1.5 = −0.125BB (still slightly negative, recovered postflop), but you can raise the open frequency toward 100% because the BB's fold rate lifts steal profit. Conversely, if the BB 3Bets frequently, narrow your range and reduce the marginal hands that only fold after a 3Bet.

Counterintuitive point: the HU button "opening near 100%" isn't greed but math. But note — opening wide doesn't mean investing every street. Postflop, adjust by board fit and let go in time — that's the mature "participate a lot, invest little" play.

Button opening quick check: default min-raise 2BB, opening about 80%-100%; top 15% strong hands + middle suited connectors/Ax + bottom junk mixed. Every 50 hands check: is the BB's 3Bet driving you out of the opening range? Does the BB's fold rate support opening to 100%?
l4hu-ev-adjustments: Heads-Up Pots: EV Calculation Simplified and Amplified

HU has only two-player pots, so EV calculation is simpler than full ring, but the numeric meaning is amplified. Simplified: no multiway splitting, no "one of my outs gives another opponent a flush" dilution — your equity is closer to "equity vs a single range". Amplified: dead money share is high (SB 0.5) and the opponent's range is wide, so the same EV differences are repeated at high frequency in HU, accumulating into bigger long-term returns. Understanding these two changes is the core of HU EV adjustments.
The core HU EV formula is unchanged, but the inputs are clearer: EV(call) = E×(P+B) − (1−E)×B. The difference is "wider opponent range, higher dead-money share", turning more marginal calls +EV.
Preflop Steal EV and Postflop Positional EV

Preflop steal EV (SB min-raise to 2BB, BB fold rate f):
EV(steal) = f×1 − (1−f)×1.5

Postflop positional EV anchor:
HU positional value about 0.5-1BB/hand (the BB is IP postflop every hand)

Example: BB facing an SB min-raise calls 1BB to contest 2BB:
Required equity = 1/(2+1) ≈ 33.3%
Marginal hands often have 40%+ vs the SB's ~80% opening range → call is +EV

The practical meaning of HU EV adjustments: against the SB's wide range, the BB's call bar drops sharply. Full ring's 40% call line vs a 15% UTG range drops to about 33% in HU vs an 80% SB range, and with positional advantage the actual equity is even higher. That's why the HU BB can defend 60%+ — not "loose" but "the result of EV calculation".

Example: HU blinds 0.5/1, preflop SB min-raises 2BB, you (BB) hold K♠7♠. Calling 1BB contests the SB's 2BB, required equity 33.3%. K7s has about 48% equity vs the SB's ~80% opening range — a surplus of about 15 points. Postflop you're IP: a K lets you bet thin value, flushes/straights chase cheaply, and a complete miss can fold. The call is +EV — full-ring K7s vs UTG is a fold, but HU vs the SB's wide range it's a +EV call.

Example 2 (postflop EV decision): Flop pot 4BB, you (BB IP) hold 7♠6♠, the SB (OOP) bets 2BB (half pot). Required equity to call = 2/(4+2+2) = 25%. Your 76 on a 9♠8♦3♣ board has a double-gutshot + backdoor flush, about 8 outs at 17% single-street — not enough at 25% alone, but adding implied odds (win 2.5BB more when the straight hits) turns the call +EV. HU draw calls rely more on implied odds because the opponent's range is wide with high payment willingness.

Counterintuitive point: in HU "small cards" aren't junk. 9-high can still win postflop in HU — the opponent's calling range is extremely wide, so 9-high's showdown value far exceeds full ring. At the same 25% pot odds, 9-high may be ahead 40%+ of the time in HU vs only 15%-20% in full ring.
HU EV quick anchors: half-pot bet needs 25%, 1/3 pot 20%, full pot 33.3%; limp to see a flop 25%, call a 3BB open 33.3%. Memorize these — faster than counting at the table.
l4hu-gto-basics: Heads-Up: The Purest Application of Equilibrium Strategy

HU poker (ignoring rake) is a pure two-player zero-sum game, where the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee strictly holds. This means HU has an equilibrium strategy (GTO): no matter how the opponent plays, your long-term expectation is never below the game value. Compared with full ring, HU GTO ranges are extremely wide (SB opens about 80%, BB defends 60%+), and equilibrium means very high betting frequency and bluff density — GTO isn't "playing tight" but "keeping everything at ratios the opponent can't counter".

HU GTO's positioning is a "bulletproof vest", not a "weapon": it guarantees you're not exploited but doesn't promise maximum profit. Against a leaky opponent, targeted exploitation earns more — at the cost of opening your own leaks. HU pros switch between "wearing the vest" and "switching to the knife".
Frequency Baselines: Value:Bluff Ratio and MDF

Equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a river full-pot bet (pot P, bet P):
Bluff share f = b/(1+2b) = 1/(1+2) = 1/3
So value:bluff = 2:1.

Half pot (b=0.5): f = 0.5/2 = 25%, value:bluff = 3:1.

MDF (Minimum Defense Frequency) = 1/(1+b):
half pot → 67%; full pot → 50%; 2× pot → 33%.

The HU BB defending 60%+ far exceeds the MDF floor (about 33%-38%) because postflop position makes calling itself +EV.

The frequency difference between HU GTO and full-ring GTO: in full ring most positions can only play tight with low equilibrium betting frequencies; HU has wide ranges, high betting frequencies, and high bluff density. Solvers output lots of aggressive bets and polarized ranges in HU. Understanding these baselines is the prerequisite for recognizing "when the opponent deviates from equilibrium".

Example: In an HU SB vs BB solver, the SB opens about 80%, the BB defends about 60%+, the OOP SB checks at high frequency postflop, and the IP BB bets at high frequency. These frequencies look "loose" but are all part of equilibrium — any deviation by one side (e.g. the SB opening only 50%) lets the other exploit it by widening defense or raising steal frequency.

Example 2 (positional symmetry): In HU the two sides swap SB/BB every hand — position isn't fixed: the SB acts last preflop (has preflop position) and first postflop (OOP); the BB is the opposite. The GTO equilibrium includes positional strategies in both directions; the symmetry means you must play both the SB and the BB, not think with full ring's "fixed position".

Counterintuitive point: "GTO is playing tight" is the biggest misreading. HU GTO is full of high-frequency betting, overbet shoves, and thin value — it just keeps all of it at ratios the opponent can't counter. When studying solvers, don't memorize frequencies — ask three whys: why this sizing on this board? Why is this hand in the betting range? Why did the frequency change on the turn?

HU GTO learning path: first use a solver to understand the equilibrium "shape" (why play this way), then use node locking to study "harvest schemes for common opponent leaks", finally validate live. The baseline gives you invincibility; deviations give you profit.
l4hu-counter-strategies: Identifying Deviations: The Prerequisite of HU Counter-Strategies

The core of HU counter-strategy is: first identify the opponent's deviations from equilibrium, then calibrate with the GTO baseline the optimal response against that leak. The four common HU deviations: folds too much (super-high fold rate vs C-Bets), calls too loose (calling station), 3Bets too often, C-Bets too often. Identification relies on 50-100 hand frequency statistics, not single-hand impressions.

The right posture of countering: aim the direction at the opponent's leak (Maximally Exploitative), keep the magnitude minimal (Minimally Exploitative). Every deviation opens your own leaks, so keep the magnitude controlled and return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.
Targeted Counters for the Four Deviations

Raising steals against an over-folding opponent (SB min-raise to 2BB, BB fold rate f):
EV(steal) = f×1 − (1−f)×1.5

Equilibrium fold rate about 40% (f=0.4) → EV = 0.4×1 − 0.6×1.5 = −0.5BB (unprofitable, recovered postflop)
At 60% fold rate (f=0.6) → EV = 0.6×1 − 0.4×1.5 = +0BB (pure steal near break-even)
At 70% (f=0.7) → EV = 0.7×1 − 0.3×1.5 = +0.25BB (auto-profit)

Conclusion: the higher the opponent's fold rate, the more your steal frequency should rise, but capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 50%".

The counter directions for the four deviations: (1) folds too much → raise open/C-Bet frequency with more semi-bluffs; (2) calls too loose (station) → cut pure bluffs, switch to value-bet thin value (top pair weak kicker bets for money); (3) 3Bets too often → narrow the open range and add 4Bet value; (4) C-Bets too often → raise x/r frequency and float. Each advances in a "identify → counter → re-check" loop.

Example: You observe a HU opponent who folds to C-Bets at 60% (equilibrium ~45%). That's a clear over-folding leak. Counter: raise your flop C-Bet frequency and bluff density overall, even adding weak hands that originally checked to the betting range. But cap it at "I still don't lose if he tightens to 50%" — this is "using GTO as the baseline and making directed, disciplined deviations from observable biases".

Example 2 (countering a station): The opponent almost never folds postflop (fold rate <25%). Counter: no pure bluffs (he doesn't fold); switch to value-bet thin value — top pair weak kicker also bets for money because he calls with worse. Meanwhile convert bluffs to semi-bluffs or checks. A station is the easiest HU type to extract from, as long as you can resist bluffing.

Example 3 (node locking in practice): In a solver, lock "this opponent folds to turn double-barrels 55%" as a fixed frequency and re-solve your optimal response — the solver immediately pushes your turn bluff frequency higher. That's node locking turning countering from "feel" into "calculation".

Counterintuitive point: the biggest risk of countering isn't "countering too little" but "over-countering and becoming the leak yourself". HU pros always keep one hand on the GTO baseline wheel while harvesting — the moment the opponent adjusts, they snap back.

Counter execution in five steps: (1) HUD-collect enough samples to confirm the leak; (2) lock the node in a solver for the optimal response; (3) compare to baseline and mark the pushed-up frequencies and sizes; (4) execute live; (5) re-check the sample every 500 hands.
l5hu-focus: Heads-Up: The Ultimate Test of Decision Density

HU is the highest-decision-density poker format: you're in a blind every hand, 200+ hands/hour, and nearly every hand sees a flop. This means your focus in HU is both a weapon and a weakness — one lapse can miss the opponent's tendencies, miscalculate odds, or lose emotional control during high-frequency downswings. HU pros treat focus as a trainable resource, not innate talent.

HU focus isn't "staring at the screen" but "maintaining the same quality across high-frequency decisions". Use session-length limits + state awareness + fatigue control so the last hand's decision quality matches the first.

HU state-management three principles: (1) session-length limit — HU focus is hard to sustain beyond 60-90 minutes; preset the time and stop on schedule, avoiding fatigue-induced decision deterioration; (2) variance budget — pause and review after losing 40-50BB, a stop-and-restart not a chase; (3) stand up every 100 hands — break losing-streak inertia and rest your eyes and mind. Fatigue signs include: starting to play marginal hands, losing bet-sizing control, repeating low-level mistakes, and ignoring the opponent's obvious tendencies.

Example: You've played HU for 2 hours straight; in the last 30 hands you've been "auto-playing" — not noticing the BB's fold rate vs your C-Bets dropped from 45% to 30%. That's a classic fatigue sign: your awareness of opponent deviations dulled and you still bet at the old frequency, getting harvested by the opponent's counter-adjustment. Correct move: pause immediately, recognize fatigue, rest, and restart with "how is the opponent playing now" rather than "how do I usually play".

Example 2 (state-management flow): Set three rules before the HU session: (1) maximum 90 minutes; (2) stop at 50BB down; (3) stand up 2 minutes every 100 hands. Execute strictly on schedule even when the table is hot — because "winners also give the edge back when tired". Tendler emphasizes: discipline isn't limiting fun but protecting long-term EV.

Counterintuitive point: the most dangerous thing in HU isn't "impulse when losing" but "letting your guard down after winning". After winning a few hands, players often relax, play marginal hands, and give the edge back. HU discipline must be consistent throughout, win or lose.
HU session-management triad: (1) preset a variance budget — pause and review after losing 40-50BB; (2) stand up every 100 hands to break losing-streak inertia; (3) review only EV, never results.
l5hu-opponent-psychology: Heads-Up: The Battlefield of Reading People

HU faces one opponent, so reading people is amplified enormously — you don't juggle multiple table images, just this one player. Opponent psychology (Reading) splits into two types: behavior patterns (bet sizes, calling tendencies, tilt tendencies) and real-time signals (bet rhythm, reaction time). In HU the two combine to help you infer the opponent's range and emotional state.

Reading isn't guessing hands — it's estimating ranges + emotions. "Calls too fast" may mean a marginal or strong hand; "thinks too long" may mean a tough decision or acting. Convert observations into probabilities, not certainties.
Reading Bet Rhythm and Reaction Time

Bet rhythm and reaction time are important signals in HU (especially online). Common readings: betting too fast = possibly a strong hand (eager for value) or a weak hand (not wanting to overthink); thinking too long = a tough decision (marginal hand/draw) or acting; hesitant calls = marginal hands. But these signals are unreliable with insufficient samples — cross-verify with 50-100 hand frequency statistics; a single rhythm doesn't count.

Example: The HU opponent thinks 20 seconds before calling your turn bet. Frequency read: long think = a tough decision, possibly a marginal hand (station trait) or a draw. But with insufficient samples it could be acting. Correct approach is cross-verification: his tendency to call big bets, his river showdown choices — judge comprehensively rather than relying on one rhythm alone.

Example 2 (counter-reading): You hold AA and watch your rhythm when betting the flop. If you bet instantly because "I have a strong hand" and hesitate because "I'm bluffing", the opponent will quickly crack you. Counter-reading drill: set the same think time for all bets, or deliberately break rhythm at key moments (hesitate with strong, be decisive with bluffs). You read the opponent, and the opponent reads you.

Counterintuitive point: the enemy of reads isn't "reading wrong" but "overconfidence". HU pros admit "this read is only 60% sure" and bet accordingly, rather than "I know what he has". Converting reads into probabilities rather than certainties is the sustainable strategy.

Read discipline: (1) only conclude from statistically significant frequencies (50+ hand samples); (2) cross-verify bet rhythm with frequency; (3) admit read uncertainty and fold it into equity and pot-odds calculations. After these three, reads go from mysticism to math.
l6hu-tourney: HU Tournaments: The Game of Chips and Blinds

HU tournaments (SNG final table / MTT heads-up) differ from ante-structure, fixed-depth cash games: blinds rise over time, chips are a finite resource, and ICM pressure dominates decisions. In HU tournaments, chip rhythm becomes the core — deep stacks (40BB+) can maintain cash-style postflop play, while shallow stacks (under 20BB) shift to preflop shove games.

The golden rule of HU tournaments: the shallower the stack and the higher the blind share, the more frequent preflop shoves. ICM and blind pressure make "survival" and "aggression" equally important goals.

The ICM at an HU SNG final table is simple: the winner takes all the prize, so ICM pressure is lower than full ring but still affects decisions — you avoid unnecessary variance when deep (protecting the lead) and use high aggression to double when behind. Blind attack/defense: shallow-stacked (like 15-20BB), the min-raise steal + shove becomes the main weapon because rising blinds make your steals auto-profit; while cash's complex postflop play fails at shallow stacks.

Example: HU SNG final table, you have 18BB vs the opponent's 22BB, blinds 0.5/1. You (SB) hold A♠4♠. At this depth, A4s is in the standard push/shove range: about 50% equity vs the BB's ~60% calling range, the 18BB shove is +EV, and rising blinds lower the value of waiting. Deep-stacked (60BB+), A4s is still an open but with more postflop room. Stack depth directly changes how the same hand plays.

Example 2 (the urgency of rising blinds): HU MTT final, blinds rise every 5 minutes and you drop from 30BB to 12BB. Now "waiting for good cards" is wrong — rising blinds spike your waiting cost. The correct strategy is raising shove frequency, using any hand with equity (pairs, Ax, strong suited connectors) to steal and double. The key to chip rhythm: act before the blinds devour you.

Counterintuitive point: the ICM logic of "conservative when ahead, aggressive when behind" in HU tournaments differs from cash's "always max EV". When deep and ahead, avoid big variance; when behind, double aggressively — because in a tournament only first place matters.

HU tournament chip-rhythm quick memory: (1) 40BB+ deep stacks maintain cash-style play; (2) 20-40BB medium stacks, min-raise + postflop; (3) under 15BB shallow stacks, shoves dominate. Re-evaluate your strategy after every blind rise — don't let the old rhythm hurt you.
l7hu-stakes:
Heads-Up is poker's purest form. Compared with 6-max or full ring, HU has these characteristics:

1. Bigger positional value: the BTN has positional advantage every hand
2. Much wider ranges: any pair is strong, any Ax is strong
3. More frequent postflop decisions: more often only two players contest the pot
4. More important exploitative adjustments: you can quickly identify and exploit opponent weaknesses
Core concept: positional value is huge in HU. The BTN has positional advantage every hand. Any pair is strong in HU, and any Ax is strong.

HU preflop ranges are much wider than 6-max:

BTN open range: about 50-70% (vs 6-max's 30-40%)
- Any pair is strong
- Any Ax is strong
- Suited connectors and small pairs can all open

3-Bet range:
- Wider (about 10-15%)
- Includes strong hands + some bluffs
- Balance matters more

The key HU postflop adjustments:

1. More C-Bets: the BTN has range advantage and should C-Bet at high frequency
2. Wider value bets: top pair weak kicker is also a strong hand
3. More bluffs: the opponent's range is wider, easier to bluff off
4. Positional use: with position you can value-bet and bluff more frequently
Adapting to Different HU Opponent Types

Quickly identify HU opponent types and adjust:

1. Tight-passive: C-Bet frequently, bluff more
2. Loose-passive: value-bet more, bluff less
3. Loose-aggressive: balanced play, some traps
4. Tight-aggressive: respect the opponent, avoid excessive conflict
The most important HU skill is quickly identifying the opponent type and adjusting. Build a basic portrait in the first 20 hands, then start exploiting.
Warning: don't play HU with 6-max standards. Many hands that are folds in 6-max are calls or raises in HU.
l8hu-exploitative: HU Exploitation: Not Abandoning GTO, Calibrating It

HU exploitative play profits from the opponent's deviations from equilibrium. But HU pros don't "abandon" GTO; they "calibrate" it: using equilibrium frequencies as the baseline and making minimum necessary deviations against the opponent's clear deviations. HU is the format where reading people is most valuable — facing one opponent, you can quickly identify his leaks and harvest with targeted strategies.

The right posture of exploitation: aim the direction at the opponent's leak (Maximally Exploitative), keep the magnitude minimal (Minimally Exploitative). Every deviation opens your own leaks, so keep the magnitude controlled and return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.
Frequency Reading: From Statistics to Exploitation

Frequency reading is the foundation of HU exploitation: identify the opponent's four-dimensional tendencies (open rate, fold rate vs C-Bets, 3Bet rate, showdown tendency), then harvest with targeted strategies. Folds too much → raise C-Bet/steal frequency; calls too loose (station) → value-bet thin value and cut pure bluffs; 3Bets too often → narrow the open and add 4Bet; C-Bets too often → raise x/r. Identification relies on 50-100 hand statistics; single-hand impressions don't count.

Example: You observe a HU opponent who folds to C-Bets at 62% (equilibrium ~45%). That's a clear over-folding leak. Exploit: raise your flop C-Bet frequency and bluff density overall, even adding weak hands that originally checked to the betting range. But cap it at "I still don't lose if he tightens to 50%" — keeping correction room. That's a "directed, disciplined deviation".

Example 2 (range polarization): Against a station who calls too loose, polarize your betting range — bet value with the nuts, semi-bluff with strong draws, check middle hands. Because the station calls with weak hands, your wide value range gets overpaid. Meanwhile cut pure bluffs (he doesn't fold) and convert bluffs to semi-bluffs or checks.

Example 3 (dynamic adjustment): After you raise steal frequency, the opponent starts 3Betting frequently — he's discovered your deviation. Now you must return to the GTO baseline (narrow the steal range, reduce pure bluffs), or your newly opened leaks get harvested in reverse. Exploitation is a dynamic game: deviate → get detected → return to baseline, looping.

Counterintuitive point: the biggest risk of exploitation isn't "exploiting too little" but "over-exploiting and becoming the leak yourself". HU pros always keep one hand on the GTO baseline wheel while harvesting — the moment the opponent adjusts, they snap back.

Exploitation execution in five steps: (1) HUD-collect enough samples to confirm the leak; (2) lock the node in a solver for the optimal response; (3) compare to baseline and mark the pushed-up frequencies and sizes; (4) execute live; (5) re-check the sample every 500 hands. A "lock" without data support is exploitation on paper.

l3hu-bn-aggression-q1.question: The core frequency advantage of the HU button (SB) is:
options: Acting last preflop, with one more piece of information every hand
Seeing the flop for free every hand
l3hu-bn-aggression-q1.explanation: The HU SB acts last preflop (has preflop position) — its core advantage; postflop it actually acts first (OOP). C is the SB completing the blind to see the flop, not an "act-last advantage".

l3hu-bn-aggression-q2.question: The typical HU button (SB) opening frequency is about:
l3hu-bn-aggression-q2.explanation: The HU SB opens about 80% because there's only one opponent, any pair and Ax are strong, and it acts last preflop. 100% is close but not GTO (some junk still folds).

l3hu-bn-aggression-q3.question: On a dry high board (K♠7♦2♣), the HU button C-Bet tendency is:
l3hu-bn-aggression-q3.explanation: The opponent rarely hits a dry high board; 1/3-pot small bets steal pots and bet thin value at high frequency — the standard play. Overbets/only-nuts waste the frequency advantage.

l3hu-bn-aggression-q4.question: The correct meaning of "constant pressure" on the HU button is:
options: Seize initiative with high-frequency opens and C-Bets, but mix checks on wet boards to keep the x/r lever
l3hu-bn-aggression-q4.explanation: Constant pressure is a frequency advantage, not mindless firing. Mixing checks on wet boards or when the turn changes hands keeps the x/r lever — the correct posture.

l3hu-bn-aggression-q5.question: The math basis for the HU button opening about 80% is:
options: Any pair and Ax are strong against one opponent
l3hu-bn-aggression-q5.explanation: HU faces only one opponent; any pair, Ax, and suited connectors have enough equity against a wide range, plus acting last preflop — hence high-frequency opens.

l3hu-sb-continuation-q1.question: The HU SB acts first postflop (OOP); its C-Bet core characteristic is:
options: Relying on board range advantage, mixing checks to keep the x/r lever
l3hu-sb-continuation-q1.explanation: The SB is OOP postflop so C-Bets cost more. The correct posture is setting frequency by board range advantage and mixing checks to keep the x/r lever.

l3hu-sb-continuation-q2.question: On a dry high board (K♠7♦2♣), the SB's (OOP) C-Bet frequency tendency is:
l3hu-sb-continuation-q2.explanation: The SB's opening range holds plenty of Kx on a dry board — clear range advantage; 1/3-pot small bets at high frequency make the BB's weak hands fold or bet thin value.

l3hu-sb-continuation-q3.question: On a wet connected board (9♠8♥6♣), the SB's (OOP) C-Bet frequency should:
options: Drop sharply (about 30%-40%) because the BB has nut advantage
l3hu-sb-continuation-q3.explanation: The BB's defense range holds many straights/draws on wet boards with the nut advantage tilted to the BB — the SB should lower frequency and mix checks for pot control.

l3hu-sb-continuation-q4.question: The correct understanding of an OOP check in HU is:
options: Handing the decision to the IP and keeping the x/r lever — a mature play
l3hu-sb-continuation-q4.explanation: An OOP check isn't weakness but kicking the ball to the IP and deciding whether to accept, while keeping the x/r lever — the mature HU SB posture.

l3hu-sb-continuation-q5.question: The SB holding an overpair on a wet board (9♠8♥6♣) should:
options: 2/3+ pot big bets to protect equity, while weak hands check for pot control
l3hu-sb-continuation-q5.explanation: An overpair on a wet board is ahead but easily outdrawn — use 2/3-pot big bets to protect; simultaneously weak hands in the range check to build a balanced bet/check structure.

l3hu-bb-defense-q1.question: The typical HU BB defense frequency vs an SB open is about:
l3hu-bb-defense-q1.explanation: The HU BB defends about 60%-70% (calls about 35%-50% + 3Bets about 15%-25%). 15%-25% is a tight full-ring magnitude; 85%-95% is a passive calling station.

l3hu-bb-defense-q2.question: The math basis for the HU BB defending 60%+ is:
options: The BB has better cards every hand
The BB is IP postflop and calls are cheap (SB dead money)
The BB must stop the SB from stealing with any cards
l3hu-bb-defense-q2.explanation: The BB is IP postflop with equity realization over 100%, and the SB's 0.5 dead money makes calls cheap — so it can defend above the MDF floor and still profit.

l3hu-bb-defense-q3.question: On a wet board (8♣5♦2♠), the BB holding a strong draw facing the SB's C-Bet should:
l3hu-bb-defense-q3.explanation: A strong draw (double-gutshot + backdoor flush) is a standard x/r semi-bluff: the SB folding wins it directly, and when called there's improvement room while suppressing the SB's C-Bet frequency.

l3hu-bb-defense-q4.question: The BB holding top pair top kicker on a dry board facing an SB C-Bet should:
options: Check-raise to scare off weak hands
Call, keeping the SB's bluffs and pot-controlling in position
l3hu-bb-defense-q4.explanation: IP top pair tends toward calling rather than x/r: calling keeps the SB's bluffs and lets you control later streets in position; an x/r instead scares off weak hands and wastes thin value.

l3hu-bb-defense-q5.question: The difference between the HU BB's "60%+ defense" and a "calling station" is:
options: The BB's defense consists of calls, 3Bet value, 3Bet bluffs, and x/r with structure; a station has none of these levers
The BB's defense is more passive
l3hu-bb-defense-q5.explanation: The BB's 60% is a "structured choice" (including 3Bet and x/r levers), while a station is passive "reluctant to fold". Defense width ≠ defense passivity.

l4hu-bn-opening-q1.question: The HU button (SB) opening frequency range is about:
l4hu-bn-opening-q1.explanation: The HU SB opens about 80%-100%, folding only a few completely junk hands — because completing 0.5 sees a 1.5BB pot and it acts last preflop.

l4hu-bn-opening-q2.question: Why does the HU button open mainly with min-raise (2BB)?
options: The min-raise steal bar is low (60% fold rate) and postflop pot control is easier
The min-raise makes the opponent fold more easily
l4hu-bn-opening-q2.explanation: The min-raise's steal break-even is a 60% fold rate, the small size makes postflop pot control easier, and it supports a ~80% wide range. Big sizes are self-punishment in HU.

l4hu-bn-opening-q3.question: The real HU BB fold rate vs min-raise is about:
l4hu-bn-opening-q3.explanation: The HU BB's real fold rate vs min-raise is only about 30%-40% (defending 60%-70%), meaning pure stealing barely profits — the open's value is postflop.

l4hu-bn-opening-q4.question: The correct understanding of the HU button "opening about 80%" is:
options: Participate in about 80%, but many hands let go in time by postflop board fit
Only play the top 80% strong hands
l4hu-bn-opening-q4.explanation: Opening wide means "participate a lot, invest little" — letting go in time by postflop board fit is the mature play.

l4hu-bn-opening-q5.question: Against a BB who 3Bets frequently, the button should adjust its open by:
options: Narrowing the range, reducing marginal hands that only fold after a 3Bet
l4hu-bn-opening-q5.explanation: High 3Bet frequency erodes steal EV and marginal hands only fold after a 3Bet. Narrowing is correct; stopping entirely overreacts.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q1.question: The main difference between HU and full-ring EV calculation is:
options: No multiway dilution, high dead-money share, wide opponent range — the EV numbers are amplified
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q1.explanation: The EV formula is unchanged, but HU two-player pots have no dilution, the SB's dead money share is high, and the opponent's range is wide — turning more marginal calls +EV and amplifying the meaning.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q2.question: SB min-raises to 2BB; the BB calls 1BB to contest the SB's 2BB. Required equity is about:
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q2.explanation: Required equity = 1/(2+1) ≈ 33.3%. HU's dead-money share is higher, cheaper than the full-ring BTN call at 40%.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q3.question: The root reason the HU BB defends 60%+ is:
options: The call bar is low vs the SB's wide range and positional advantage makes actual equity higher
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q3.explanation: Vs the SB's ~80% wide range the call bar drops to about 33%, and IP equity realization exceeds 100% — hence wide defense, the result of EV calculation rather than "looseness".

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q4.question: HU draw calls (like double-gutshots) rely on implied odds because:
options: The opponent's range is wide with high payment willingness — winning more when the draw hits
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q4.explanation: The HU opponent's range is wide with high payment willingness, so you win more when the draw hits (good implied odds), compensating for the single-street equity shortfall.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q5.question: HU positional value of about 0.5-1BB/hand means:
options: The BB wins 1BB more every flop
Over the long run the BB earns 0.5-1BB more expected value per hand than the SB
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q5.explanation: Positional value is a long-run expectation gap: the BB's postflop information advantage averages 0.5-1BB extra per hand — a statistical expectation, not a per-hand guarantee.

l4hu-gto-basics-q1.question: The applicability of the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee in HU:
options: Strictly holds (HU is a pure two-player zero-sum game)
l4hu-gto-basics-q1.explanation: HU (ignoring rake) is a pure two-player zero-sum game, where the Nash unexploitable guarantee strictly holds. Multiway pots weaken under coalition effects.

l4hu-gto-basics-q2.question: The equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a river full-pot bet is about:
l4hu-gto-basics-q2.explanation: Bluff share f = 1/(1+2) = 1/3, so 2/3 value and 1/3 bluffs, value:bluff = 2:1. Exactly equals the opponent's required call equity of 33%.

l4hu-gto-basics-q3.question: The main difference between HU GTO and full-ring GTO is:
options: HU ranges are extremely wide with high betting frequencies and bluff density
l4hu-gto-basics-q3.explanation: HU ranges are wide (SB 80%, BB 60%+), so equilibrium comes with high betting frequencies and polarized ranges — not "playing tight".

l4hu-gto-basics-q4.question: Why does the HU BB defend 60%+, far above the MDF floor (about 33%-38%)?
options: The BB has better cards every hand
The MDF formula doesn't apply preflop
l4hu-gto-basics-q4.explanation: MDF only guarantees "stopping pure-bluff auto-profit"; the BB's call +EV comes from postflop position (equity realization >100%), so it can defend above the floor and still profit.

l4hu-gto-basics-q5.question: HU "positional symmetry" means:
options: Every hand the two sides swap SB/BB — you must play both the SB and the BB
l4hu-gto-basics-q5.explanation: In HU the two sides swap SB/BB every hand (SB acts last preflop/first postflop; BB the opposite); the GTO equilibrium includes positional strategies in both directions.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q1.question: The correct basis for identifying a HU opponent's deviation is:
l4hu-counter-strategies-q1.explanation: HU countering relies on 50-100 hand frequency statistics (fold rate/3Bet rate, etc.); single-hand impressions are noise, insufficient evidence.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q2.question: Against an over-folding opponent, the correct counter is:
options: Raise open/C-Bet frequency and add semi-bluffs
l4hu-counter-strategies-q2.explanation: An over-folding opponent makes steal and C-Bet fold rates automatic profit — raise open/C-Bet frequency and semi-bluff density.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q3.question: Against a calling station who calls too loose, the correct counter is:
options: Cut bluffs and switch to value-bet thin value
l4hu-counter-strategies-q3.explanation: A station doesn't fold, so pure bluffs are useless; switch to value-bet thin value because he calls with worse hands.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q4.question: The discipline of "minimum necessary deviation" is:
options: Aiming at the opponent's leak with minimal magnitude, ready to return to baseline anytime
l4hu-counter-strategies-q4.explanation: Deviations open your own leaks, so keep the magnitude controlled; aim at the leak, keep it minimal, and return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q5.question: The role of node locking in countering is:
options: Locking the opponent's deviation as a fixed frequency and re-solving your optimal response
l4hu-counter-strategies-q5.explanation: Node locking feeds "how the opponent actually plays (deviation)" into the solver and outputs the optimal counter against that bias — turning countering from feel into calculation.

l5hu-focus-q1.question: The core of HU focus is:
options: Staring at the screen without distraction
Maintaining the same quality across high-frequency decisions, via session limits and fatigue control
l5hu-focus-q1.explanation: HU focus is "maintaining quality across high-frequency decisions", achieved through state management like session-length limits, variance budgets, and periodic breaks.

l5hu-focus-q2.question: The reasonable upper limit of an HU session length is about:
l5hu-focus-q2.explanation: HU focus is hard to sustain beyond 60-90 minutes; overtime causes decision deterioration. Fatigue risk is extremely high beyond 3 hours.

l5hu-focus-q3.question: Which is NOT a typical fatigue sign?
options: Being more aware of opponent tendencies
l5hu-focus-q3.explanation: Fatigue dulls awareness of opponent tendencies rather than sharpening it. Marginal hands, sizing control loss, and low-level mistakes are fatigue signs.

l5hu-focus-q4.question: The role of the "pause at 50BB" variance budget is:
options: Limiting the maximum you can lose
Pausing for review at the stop-loss point, avoiding chase-style re-buying
l5hu-focus-q4.explanation: A variance budget is stop-loss discipline: pause and review at the preset point, cutting the "get even" impulse and avoiding fatigue and tilt.

l5hu-focus-q5.question: The correct statement about HU discipline is:
options: You can extend time when the table is hot
Discipline must be consistent throughout, win or lose
Discipline is only needed when losing
l5hu-focus-q5.explanation: Relaxation after winning and fatigue are equally dangerous. HU discipline must be consistent throughout — no relaxation in either direction — to protect long-term EV.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q1.question: The correct way to read people in HU is:
options: Estimating ranges + emotions, converting observations into probabilities
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q1.explanation: Reading is estimating ranges + emotions, converting observations into probabilities rather than certainties. Single-hand impressions are unreliable.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q2.question: The common reading of "betting too fast" in HU is:
options: Possibly strong (eager for value) or weak (not wanting to overthink) — cross-verify
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q2.explanation: Betting too fast may be strong (eager for value) or weak (not wanting to overthink); a single signal is unreliable and needs cross-verification with frequency statistics.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q3.question: The online HU opponent thinks 20 seconds before calling your turn bet. The most reliable handling is:
options: Judge him marginal and raise immediately
Cross-verify with his tendency to call big bets and his showdown choices
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q3.explanation: A long think may mean marginal/draw/acting; a single instance is unreliable. Cross-verify with frequency like his big-bet call tendency and river showdown choices.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q4.question: The core of "counter-reading (Balanced Play)" is:
options: Making actions not leak range information, keeping rhythm consistent or breaking it
Making the opponent unable to guess hand strength
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q4.explanation: Counter-reading requires actions not to leak range: no "fast with strong, slow with weak" — keep rhythm consistent or deliberately break it.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q5.question: The correct attitude toward HU reads is:
options: Admitting uncertainty and folding it into equity and pot-odds calculations
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q5.explanation: Reads carry uncertainty; pros convert them into probabilities (like "60% sure") and fold them into decisions — the sustainable strategy.

l6hu-tourney-q1.question: The core difference between HU tournaments and cash is:
options: Blinds rise, chips are finite, ICM pressure dominates
l6hu-tourney-q1.explanation: HU tournaments have rising blinds, finite chips, and ICM pressure, with strategy adjusting dynamically by stack depth.

l6hu-tourney-q2.question: The correct strategy at HU tournament shallow stacks (under 15BB) is:
options: Preflop shoves dominate, stealing with any hand with equity
l6hu-tourney-q2.explanation: At shallow stacks preflop shoves become the main weapon because rising blinds make steals auto-profit and waiting costs spike.

l6hu-tourney-q3.question: The ICM characteristic of an HU SNG final table is:
options: Extremely high ICM pressure, near full ring
The winner takes all; ICM pressure is relatively low but still affects decisions
ICM only exists on the bubble
l6hu-tourney-q3.explanation: The HU final-table winner takes all, so ICM pressure is relatively low vs full ring but still affects decisions — avoid variance when deep, double aggressively when behind.

l6hu-tourney-q4.question: The effect of rising blinds on HU tournament strategy is:
options: Waiting costs spike — raise action frequency rather than waiting for cards
l6hu-tourney-q4.explanation: Rising blinds spike your waiting cost; the correct strategy is raising shove/steal frequency and acting before the blinds devour you.

l6hu-tourney-q5.question: The strategy at the 20-40BB medium-stack stage of HU tournaments is:
options: Min-raise + postflop, balancing steal and postflop
l6hu-tourney-q5.explanation: The medium stage (20-40BB) balances steal and postflop — min-raise plus postflop is reasonable, differing from the shallow-stack shove-dominant approach.

l7hu-stakes-q1.explanation: The HU BTN open range is about 50-70%, much wider than 6-max's 30-40%.

l7hu-stakes-q2.question: Which hand type rises most in value in HU?
l7hu-stakes-q2.explanation: In HU any pair is strong and any Ax is strong — these hands rise sharply in value.

l7hu-stakes-q3.question: Against a tight-passive opponent in HU you should:
l7hu-stakes-q3.explanation: Against a tight-passive opponent C-Bet frequently and bluff more because their fold rate is high.

l7hu-stakes-q4.question: How is positional value in HU?
options: Huge — the BTN has positional advantage every hand
l7hu-stakes-q4.explanation: HU positional value is huge — the BTN has positional advantage every hand.

l7hu-stakes-q5.question: The correct play for top pair weak kicker in HU is:
l7hu-stakes-q5.explanation: HU ranges are wider, so top pair weak kicker is also a strong hand — value bet more widely.

l8hu-exploitative-q1.question: The correct basis of HU exploitation is:
options: Using GTO as the baseline and making minimum necessary deviations against clear opponent deviations
l8hu-exploitative-q1.explanation: Exploitation is "calibrating GTO" rather than abandoning it: using equilibrium frequencies as the baseline and making directed, capped deviations against opponent deviations.

l8hu-exploitative-q2.question: Against an over-folding opponent, HU exploitation is:
options: Raise C-Bet/steal frequency and bluff density
l8hu-exploitative-q2.explanation: An over-folding opponent makes steal and C-Bet fold rates automatic profit — raise C-Bet/steal frequency and bluff density.

l8hu-exploitative-q3.question: Against a station who calls too loose, the correct exploitation is:
options: Polarize the betting range, value-bet thin value, cut pure bluffs
l8hu-exploitative-q3.explanation: A station calls with weak hands so thin value bets get overpaid; pure bluffs are useless (he doesn't fold) — convert to semi-bluffs or checks.

l8hu-exploitative-q4.question: After you raise steals, the opponent starts 3Betting frequently. The correct move is:
options: Return to the GTO baseline and narrow the range
l8hu-exploitative-q4.explanation: The opponent detected your deviation and your newly opened leaks will be harvested in reverse — you must return to baseline. Exploitation is a "deviate → get detected → return" dynamic game.

l8hu-exploitative-q5.question: HU exploitation's frequency reading relies on:
l8hu-exploitative-q5.explanation: Frequency reading relies on 50-100 hand statistics (open rate/fold rate/3Bet rate/showdown tendency); single-hand impressions are noise.
